What to take from this. We never wrote down a law of refraction. We wrote down a number attached to each candidate path, differentiated it, and set the derivative to zero. The law of refraction was the output. Chapter 1.2 does the same thing when the "candidate path" is a whole function rather than a single number xxx, and the output is Newton's second law.

Worked example 2 — escape velocity, and why energy beats force here

How fast must a projectile leave the surface of a body of mass MMM and radius RRR to never return?

The force route is impractical. You would integrate mr¨=−GMm/r2m\ddot r = -GMm/r^{2}mr¨=−GMm/r2, a nonlinear second-order ODE whose right-hand side depends on the unknown r(t)r(t)r(t), and then take a limit as t→∞t\to\inftyt→∞. Try it and you will be at it for a while.

The energy route is four lines. Newtonian gravity on a particle of mass mmm is

F  =  −GMmr2 r^. \vv F \;=\; -\frac{GMm}{r^{2}}\,\hat{\vv r}. F=−r2GMm​r^.

Is it conservative? Apply test (D). Its curl vanishes, and Problem 1 does that computation for exactly this form. Its domain R3∖{0}\R^{3}\setminus\{\vv 0\}R3∖{0} is simply connected, because in three dimensions you can always slide a loop off a removed point. So a potential exists, and since ∇(1/r)=−r^/r2\nabla(1/r) = -\hat{\vv r}/r^{2}∇(1/r)=−r^/r2,

V(r)=−GMmr⟹−∇V=−GMmr2r^=F. ✓ V(r) = -\frac{GMm}{r} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad -\nabla V = -\frac{GMm}{r^{2}}\hat{\vv r} = \vv F. \ \checkmark V(r)=−rGMm​⟹−∇V=−r2GMm​r^=F. ✓

By (1.1.8), E=12mv2−GMm/rE=\half mv^{2}-GMm/rE=21​mv2−GMm/r is constant along the entire trajectory, however complicated. "Never returns" means rrr can grow without bound, and since 12mv2≥0\half mv^{2}\geq021​mv2≥0 always while −GMm/r→0−-GMm/r\to0^{-}−GMm/r→0− as r→∞r\to\inftyr→∞, this is possible exactly when E≥0E\geq0E≥0. Evaluating EEE at launch, r=Rr=Rr=R and v=vev=v_{e}v=ve​:

12mve2−GMmR  =  0⟹  ve=2GMR   \half m v_{e}^{2} - \frac{GMm}{R} \;=\; 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \boxed{\;v_{e} = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}}\;} 21​mve2​−RGMm​=0⟹ve​=R2GM​​​

For the Earth we use the measured combination GM⊕=3.986004418×1014 m3 s−2GM_{\oplus}=3.986004418\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{m^{3}\,s^{-2}}GM⊕​=3.986004418×1014m3s−2 rather than GGG and MMM separately, because GMGMGM is known to ten significant figures and GGG alone to five. With that and R=6.371×106 mR=6.371\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{m}R=6.371×106m, the escape velocity is 11 186 m s−1=11.19 km s−111\,186\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} = 11.19\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}11186ms−1=11.19kms−1. For the Moon it is 2.376 km s−12.376\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}2.376kms−1. Equivalently, since g=GM/R2g=GM/R^{2}g=GM/R2 at the surface, ve=2gRv_{e}=\sqrt{2gR}ve​=2gR​.

Three things the energy route gave you for free. First, the mass mmm cancelled, so the escape velocity is the same for a pebble and for a spacecraft. Second, the direction of launch never entered, because EEE depends on v2=v⋅vv^{2}=\vv v\cdot\vv vv2=v⋅v rather than on v\vv vv. Ignoring the ground and the atmosphere, sideways works as well as straight up, which is not remotely apparent from the force picture. Third, you never needed the trajectory at all, because conservation replaced integration.

That last point is the general moral. A conserved quantity is a first integral, which is one integration of the equation of motion already done for you. Chapter 1.4 shows where they all come from, and by then "look for the conserved quantities first" will be the standard opening move.

7 · Your turn

Problem 1 · is the inverse-square force conservative?

Let F=−k r/r3\vv F = -k\,\vv r/r^{3}F=−kr/r3, with r=∣r∣r=\abs{\vv r}r=∣r∣ and kkk constant. This is the shape of both gravity and the Coulomb force. (a) Compute ∇×F\nabla\times\vv F∇×F directly. (b) Find VVV with F=−∇V\vv F=-\nabla VF=−∇V. (c) State carefully why the domain matters, and why the conclusion here is not spoiled by the counterexample of Chapter 0.7 §2.4.

Solution

(a) Write Fx=−kx r−3F^{x} = -kx\,r^{-3}Fx=−kxr−3 and use ∂xr=x/r\partial_{x}r = x/r∂x​r=x/r (from r=x2+y2+z2r=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}}r=x2+y2+z2​). Then by the chain rule ∂x(r−3)=−3r−4⋅(x/r)=−3x r−5\partial_{x}\big(r^{-3}\big) = -3r^{-4}\cdot(x/r) = -3x\,r^{-5}∂x​(r−3)=−3r−4⋅(x/r)=−3xr−5, and

∂xFy=∂x(−ky r−3)=−ky⋅(−3x r−5)=3kxyr5. \partial_{x}F^{y} = \partial_{x}\big(-ky\,r^{-3}\big) = -ky\cdot\big(-3x\,r^{-5}\big) = \frac{3kxy}{r^{5}}. ∂x​Fy=∂x​(−kyr−3)=−ky⋅(−3xr−5)=r53kxy​.

By the symmetry of the expression in x↔yx\leftrightarrow yx↔y, ∂yFx=3kxy/r5\partial_{y}F^{x} = 3kxy/r^{5}∂y​Fx=3kxy/r5 as well, so (∇×F)z=∂xFy−∂yFx=0(\nabla\times\vv F)_{z} = \partial_{x}F^{y}-\partial_{y}F^{x}=0(∇×F)z​=∂x​Fy−∂y​Fx=0. The other two components follow by cycling x→y→z→xx\to y\to z\to xx→y→z→x, which the expression is invariant under. So ∇×F=0\nabla\times\vv F = \vv 0∇×F=0 on all of R3∖{0}\R^{3}\setminus\{\vv 0\}R3∖{0}. (Verified symbolically.)

(b) Guess a radial potential V=V(r)V=V(r)V=V(r). Then ∇V=V′(r) r^=V′(r) r/r\nabla V = V'(r)\,\hat{\vv r} = V'(r)\,\vv r/r∇V=V′(r)r^=V′(r)r/r, so we need −V′(r)/r=−k/r3-V'(r)/r = -k/r^{3}−V′(r)/r=−k/r3, i.e. V′(r)=k/r2V'(r)=k/r^{2}V′(r)=k/r2, giving

V(r)=−kr+const. V(r) = -\frac{k}{r} + \text{const}. V(r)=−rk​+const.

Check: −∇(−k/r)=k∇(1/r)=k⋅(−r^/r2)=−kr/r3=F-\nabla(-k/r) = k\nabla(1/r) = k\cdot\big(-\hat{\vv r}/r^{2}\big) = -k\vv r/r^{3} = \vv F−∇(−k/r)=k∇(1/r)=k⋅(−r^/r2)=−kr/r3=F. ✓ The additive constant is free, which is why "the potential at infinity is zero" is a choice and not a fact.

(c) Condition (D) holds. But the arrow (D)⇒\Rightarrow⇒(C) needs the domain to be simply connected, and F\vv FF is undefined at the origin, so the domain is punctured. The saving fact is dimension. Puncturing R3\R^{3}R3 leaves a simply connected region, because any loop can be slid sideways off the missing point and then contracted. Puncturing R2\R^{2}R2 does not, because a loop encircling the hole is trapped. That is exactly why Chapter 0.7's vortex field (−y,x)/(x2+y2)(-y,x)/(x^{2}+y^{2})(−y,x)/(x2+y2) has zero curl and circulation 2π2\pi2π. Same puncture, different dimension, opposite conclusion. Here the theorem applies, the potential exists globally, and gravity is conservative everywhere it is defined.

Worth adding: ∇⋅F=0\nabla\cdot\vv F=0∇⋅F=0 away from the origin as well, also verified symbolically. Both the divergence and the curl vanish on the whole domain, and yet the field is emphatically not zero. All of its source sits in the single removed point. That is where Chapter 0.9's delta function goes, and ∇2(1/r)=−4πδ3(r)\nabla^{2}(1/r) = -4\pi\delta^{3}(\vv r)∇2(1/r)=−4πδ3(r) is the statement that makes Gauss's law work.

Problem 2 · the two-body problem becomes a one-body problem

Two particles interact only with each other, by a force obeying the strong third law. (a) Show the centre of mass moves uniformly. (b) Show the relative coordinate obeys a one-body equation, and identify the mass appearing in it. (c) Show the total kinetic energy splits cleanly into the two pieces. (d) Compute the correction for hydrogen and say what it predicts.

Solution

(a) With F12\vv F_{12}F12​ the force on 1 from 2, we have m1r¨1=F12m_{1}\ddot{\vv r}_{1}=\vv F_{12}m1​r¨1​=F12​ and m2r¨2=F21=−F12m_{2}\ddot{\vv r}_{2}=\vv F_{21}=-\vv F_{12}m2​r¨2​=F21​=−F12​. Add them and the right-hand sides cancel. Define M=m1+m2M=m_{1}+m_{2}M=m1​+m2​ and R=(m1r1+m2r2)/M\vv R=(m_{1}\vv r_{1}+m_{2}\vv r_{2})/MR=(m1​r1​+m2​r2​)/M. Then MR¨=0M\ddot{\vv R}=\vv 0MR¨=0, so R(t)=R0+Vt\vv R(t)=\vv R_{0}+\vv V tR(t)=R0​+Vt. Three of the six degrees of freedom are now solved exactly and forever. That is (1.1.10) in its most useful form.

(b) Let r=r1−r2\vv r = \vv r_{1}-\vv r_{2}r=r1​−r2​. Divide each equation by its mass and subtract:

r¨=F12m1−F21m2=F12(1m1+1m2)  ⟹  μ r¨=F12, \ddot{\vv r} = \frac{\vv F_{12}}{m_{1}} - \frac{\vv F_{21}}{m_{2}} = \vv F_{12}\left(\frac{1}{m_{1}}+\frac{1}{m_{2}}\right) \;\Longrightarrow\; \mu\,\ddot{\vv r} = \vv F_{12}, r¨=m1​F12​​−m2​F21​​=F12​(m1​1​+m2​1​)⟹μr¨=F12​,

where the reduced mass is defined by 1/μ=1/m1+1/m21/\mu = 1/m_{1}+1/m_{2}1/μ=1/m1​+1/m2​, i.e. μ=m1m2/(m1+m2)\mu = m_{1}m_{2}/(m_{1}+m_{2})μ=m1​m2​/(m1​+m2​). By the strong third law F12\vv F_{12}F12​ points along r\vv rr and (for the usual forces) depends only on rrr, so this is a single particle of mass μ\muμ in a central field. The two-body problem is solved.

(c) Inverting the definitions, r1=R+(m2/M)r\vv r_{1}=\vv R + (m_{2}/M)\vv rr1​=R+(m2​/M)r and r2=R−(m1/M)r\vv r_{2}=\vv R - (m_{1}/M)\vv rr2​=R−(m1​/M)r. Then

T=12m1∣R˙+m2Mr˙∣2+12m2∣R˙−m1Mr˙∣2=12MR˙2+R˙⋅r˙ m1m2−m2m1M+12r˙2 m1m22+m2m12M2=12MR˙2  +  12μ r˙2. \begin{aligned} T &= \half m_{1}\abs{\dot{\vv R}+\tfrac{m_{2}}{M}\dot{\vv r}}^{2} + \half m_{2}\abs{\dot{\vv R}-\tfrac{m_{1}}{M}\dot{\vv r}}^{2}\\[3pt] &= \half M\dot R^{2} + \dot{\vv R}\cdot\dot{\vv r}\,\frac{m_{1}m_{2}-m_{2}m_{1}}{M} + \half\dot r^{2}\,\frac{m_{1}m_{2}^{2}+m_{2}m_{1}^{2}}{M^{2}}\\[3pt] &= \half M\dot R^{2} \;+\; \half\mu\,\dot r^{2}. \end{aligned} T​=21​m1​​R˙+Mm2​​r˙​2+21​m2​​R˙−Mm1​​r˙​2=21​MR˙2+R˙⋅r˙Mm1​m2​−m2​m1​​+21​r˙2M2m1​m22​+m2​m12​​=21​MR˙2+21​μr˙2.​

The cross terms cancel exactly, which is why R\vv RR was defined with those particular weights, and the last step used m1m2(m1+m2)/M2=μm_{1}m_{2}(m_{1}+m_{2})/M^{2}=\mum1​m2​(m1​+m2​)/M2=μ. Centre-of-mass motion and relative motion do not talk to each other, either in the equations or in the energy.

(d) For hydrogen, μ/me=mp/(mp+me)=0.999455679\mu/m_{e} = m_{p}/(m_{p}+m_{e}) = 0.999455679μ/me​=mp​/(mp​+me​)=0.999455679, a reduction of 5.44×10−45.44\times10^{-4}5.44×10−4. Every energy level scales with μ\muμ, so every spectral line shifts by that fraction. For deuterium the nucleus is about twice as heavy, giving μ/me=0.999727630\mu/m_{e}=0.999727630μ/me​=0.999727630, so the fractional difference between the two is 2.721×10−42.721\times10^{-4}2.721×10−4. Applied to the H-α\alphaα line at 656.28 nm656.28\,\mathrm{nm}656.28nm, this predicts a deuterium line shifted by 0.179 nm0.179\,\mathrm{nm}0.179nm toward the blue. That is how Urey identified deuterium in 1932, and it is a purely classical centre-of-mass effect sitting inside a quantum calculation.

Problem 3 · polar acceleration, and which terms are real

(a) Derive (1.1.35) by a route that never mentions unit vectors: write x=rcos⁡θx=r\cos\thetax=rcosθ, y=rsin⁡θy=r\sin\thetay=rsinθ, differentiate twice, and project. (b) A particle moves on a circle of fixed radius RRR at constant angular rate ω\omegaω. Compute FrF_{r}Fr​ and FθF_{\theta}Fθ​. (c) Which of the four terms in (1.1.35) would survive a change to a different coordinate system, and which are artefacts?

Solution

(a) Differentiate x=rcos⁡θx=r\cos\thetax=rcosθ twice with the product and chain rules:

x˙=r˙cos⁡θ−rθ˙sin⁡θ,x¨=r¨cos⁡θ−2r˙θ˙sin⁡θ−rθ¨sin⁡θ−rθ˙2cos⁡θ, \begin{aligned} \dot x &= \dot r\cos\theta - r\dot\theta\sin\theta,\\ \ddot x &= \ddot r\cos\theta - 2\dot r\dot\theta\sin\theta - r\ddot\theta\sin\theta - r\dot\theta^{2}\cos\theta, \end{aligned} x˙x¨​=r˙cosθ−rθ˙sinθ,=r¨cosθ−2r˙θ˙sinθ−rθ¨sinθ−rθ˙2cosθ,​

and similarly y¨=r¨sin⁡θ+2r˙θ˙cos⁡θ+rθ¨cos⁡θ−rθ˙2sin⁡θ\ddot y = \ddot r\sin\theta + 2\dot r\dot\theta\cos\theta + r\ddot\theta\cos\theta - r\dot\theta^{2}\sin\thetay¨​=r¨sinθ+2r˙θ˙cosθ+rθ¨cosθ−rθ˙2sinθ. The radial component of the acceleration is ar=x¨cos⁡θ+y¨sin⁡θa_{r}=\ddot x\cos\theta + \ddot y\sin\thetaar​=x¨cosθ+y¨​sinθ. Every term either picks up cos⁡2+sin⁡2=1\cos^{2}+\sin^{2}=1cos2+sin2=1 or the cancelling combination −cos⁡sin⁡+sin⁡cos⁡=0-\cos\sin+\sin\cos=0−cossin+sincos=0:

ar=r¨−rθ˙2. a_{r} = \ddot r - r\dot\theta^{2}. ar​=r¨−rθ˙2.

The tangential component is aθ=−x¨sin⁡θ+y¨cos⁡θa_{\theta}=-\ddot x\sin\theta+\ddot y\cos\thetaaθ​=−x¨sinθ+y¨​cosθ, and the same bookkeeping gives aθ=rθ¨+2r˙θ˙a_{\theta} = r\ddot\theta + 2\dot r\dot\thetaaθ​=rθ¨+2r˙θ˙. (Both confirmed with a computer algebra system.) Multiply by mmm and you have (1.1.35). Note that this route is longer rather than shorter. The unit-vector derivatives of (1.1.32) were doing real work.

(b) Here r=Rr=Rr=R is constant, so r˙=r¨=0\dot r=\ddot r=0r˙=r¨=0, and θ˙=ω\dot\theta=\omegaθ˙=ω is constant, so θ¨=0\ddot\theta=0θ¨=0. Then Fr=−mRω2F_{r}=-mR\omega^{2}Fr​=−mRω2 and Fθ=0F_{\theta}=0Fθ​=0. The force is purely radial and points inward. It is the centripetal force, and its magnitude mRω2=mv2/RmR\omega^{2}=mv^{2}/RmRω2=mv2/R falls out of the general formula rather than being quoted. There is no outward "centrifugal force" acting on the particle. The −rθ˙2-r\dot\theta^{2}−rθ˙2 sits on the acceleration side of the equation.

(c) None of the four terms is coordinate-independent, and that is the point. Under a change of coordinates the whole left-hand side transforms as a unit, and individual terms have no invariant meaning on their own. But there is a sharp version of the question. Write the equations in Cartesian coordinates and the extra terms are absent. Write them in polar and they are present. The physics is identical either way. Any term you can remove by relabelling the plane is not describing a physical interaction, so −mrθ˙2-mr\dot\theta^{2}−mrθ˙2 and 2mr˙θ˙2m\dot r\dot\theta2mr˙θ˙ are artefacts of the labelling. (1.1.36) makes it concrete: a free particle has r¨≠0\ddot r\neq0r¨=0.

The right way to say this, available from Chapter 3.3 onward, is that q¨i+Γijkq˙jq˙k\ddot q^{i}+\Gamma^{i}{}_{jk}\dot q^{j}\dot q^{k}q¨​i+Γijk​q˙​jq˙​k is a coordinate-independent object while q¨i\ddot q^{i}q¨​i alone is not, and the Γ\GammaΓ's are exactly the centrifugal and Coriolis terms. Gravity, remarkably, belongs to the same category. It too can be removed at a point by choosing the right coordinates, namely a freely falling frame, which is the equivalence principle of Chapter 3.1. What distinguishes gravity from centrifugal force is that no single coordinate change removes it everywhere at once, and the obstruction is curvature.

Problem 4 · the third law fails, quantitatively

Two protons (q=1.602×10−19 Cq=1.602\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}q=1.602×10−19C) are separated by d=1.00 nmd=1.00\,\mathrm{nm}d=1.00nm along x^\hat{\vv x}x^. Proton 1, at the origin, moves with v1=vx^\vv v_{1}=v\hat{\vv x}v1​=vx^, and proton 2 moves with v2=vy^\vv v_{2}=v\hat{\vv y}v2​=vy^​, where v=3.00×106 m s−1v=3.00\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}v=3.00×106ms−1. (a) Compute the magnetic force on each. (b) Compute dPmech/dt\dd\vv P_{\text{mech}}/\dd tdPmech​/dt for the pair and compare it to the Coulomb force. (c) Where is the missing momentum, and what would you have to compute to find it?

Solution

(a) The field of 1 at 2 involves v1×r^=vx^×x^=0\vv v_{1}\times\hat{\vv r}=v\hat{\vv x}\times\hat{\vv x} =\vv 0v1​×r^=vx^×x^=0, so B1(r2)=0\vv B_{1}(\vv r_{2})=\vv 0B1​(r2​)=0 and the magnetic force on proton 2 is exactly zero. For the other direction, r^\hat{\vv r}r^ from 2 to 1 is −x^-\hat{\vv x}−x^, so by (1.1.14)

B2(r1)=μ0qv4πd2 z^,F12mag=qvx^×B2=−μ0q2v24πd2 y^. \vv B_{2}(\vv r_{1}) = \frac{\mu_{0}qv}{4\pi d^{2}}\,\hat{\vv z}, \qquad \vv F_{12}^{\text{mag}} = qv\hat{\vv x}\times\vv B_{2} = -\frac{\mu_{0}q^{2}v^{2}}{4\pi d^{2}}\,\hat{\vv y}. B2​(r1​)=4πd2μ0​qv​z^,F12mag​=qvx^×B2​=−4πd2μ0​q2v2​y^​.

Numerically, with μ0/4π=10−7\mu_{0}/4\pi = 10^{-7}μ0​/4π=10−7 exactly, q2=2.566×10−38q^{2}=2.566\times10^{-38}q2=2.566×10−38, v2=9.00×1012v^{2}=9.00\times10^{12}v2=9.00×1012 and d2=10−18d^{2}=10^{-18}d2=10−18,

∣F12mag∣=10−7×2.566×10−38×9.00×101210−18=2.31×10−14 N. \abs{\vv F_{12}^{\text{mag}}} = \frac{10^{-7}\times 2.566\times10^{-38}\times 9.00\times10^{12}}{10^{-18}} = 2.31\times10^{-14}\,\mathrm{N}. ∣F12mag​∣=10−1810−7×2.566×10−38×9.00×1012​=2.31×10−14N.

(b) The Coulomb forces are equal and opposite and cancel in the sum, so the net internal force on the pair is the magnetic residue alone:

dPmechdt=F12+F21=−2.31×10−14 y^ N. \dv{\vv P_{\text{mech}}}{t} = \vv F_{12}+\vv F_{21} = -2.31\times10^{-14}\,\hat{\vv y}\ \mathrm{N}. dtdPmech​​=F12​+F21​=−2.31×10−14y^​ N.

The Coulomb force is q2/4πε0d2=8.988×109×2.566×10−38/10−18=2.307×10−10 Nq^{2}/4\pi\varepsilon_{0}d^{2} = 8.988\times10^{9}\times2.566\times10^{-38}/10^{-18} = 2.307\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{N}q2/4πε0​d2=8.988×109×2.566×10−38/10−18=2.307×10−10N, so the ratio is 1.00×10−41.00\times10^{-4}1.00×10−4. Check it against the closed form (1.1.18): both forces carry the same q2/d2q^{2}/d^{2}q2/d2, so the ratio must be μ0ε0v2=v2/c2=(3.00×106/2.998×108)2=1.00×10−4\mu_{0}\varepsilon_{0}v^{2}=v^{2}/c^{2} = \big(3.00\times10^{6}/2.998\times10^{8}\big)^{2} = 1.00\times10^{-4}μ0​ε0​v2=v2/c2=(3.00×106/2.998×108)2=1.00×10−4. ✓ The ddd-dependence cancels, so the violation is the same fractional size at any separation.

The conclusion stands regardless of the numbers. An isolated pair of particles has dP/dt≠0\dd\vv P/\dd t\neq\vv 0dP/dt=0. The effect is suppressed by v2/c2v^{2}/c^{2}v2/c2, which is why nobody noticed for two centuries, and exactly why it is a relativistic effect in disguise.

(c) It is in the electromagnetic field. To find it you would compute Pfield=ε0∫E×B  d3x\vv P_{\text{field}} = \varepsilon_{0}\int\vv E\times\vv B\;\dd^{3}xPfield​=ε0​∫E×Bd3x over all space, using the total E\vv EE and B\vv BB of both charges, and then verify that d(Pmech+Pfield)/dt=0\dd(\vv P_{\text{mech}}+\vv P_{\text{field}})/\dd t=\vv 0d(Pmech​+Pfield​)/dt=0. Chapter 2.6 derives the integrand from Maxwell's equations and proves the conservation law in general. The mechanism is the Maxwell stress tensor, which is the momentum flux through a surface, and the proof is the field-theoretic version of (1.1.10).

A further honesty note. The Biot–Savart expression we used is the leading term in v/cv/cv/c. A full treatment uses the Liénard–Wiechert fields, which are retarded: the field at charge 2 now depends on where charge 1 was d/cd/cd/c seconds ago. Retardation makes the failure of the third law inevitable rather than accidental. If the interaction is not instantaneous, then "equal and opposite at the same instant" is not even a well-posed statement, because different observers disagree about which instants are simultaneous (Chapter 2.3).

The brick you just laid

You have Newton's three laws stated with their fine print: the first as a definition of the frames in which the second holds, the second as a second-order ODE whose Picard–Lindelöf uniqueness is determinism, the third in two strengths. You know that the second law is a framework and not a theory, because it does not say what F\vv FF is.

You have energy: the work–energy theorem from one dot product, kinetic energy appearing unbidden, and E=T+VE=T+VE=T+V conserved exactly when the force is conservative in Chapter 0.7's sense. That is the machinery Chapter 1.2 is built from (L=T−VL=T-VL=T−V), Chapter 1.3 rebuilds as the Hamiltonian, and Chapter 1.4 re-derives from time-translation symmetry.

You have momentum and angular momentum from the weak and strong third laws, and you have a crack. The third law is false for magnetic forces between moving charges, momentum is not conserved among the particles alone, and the only available repair is that the field carries momentum. That is the first evidence in this book that fields are objects rather than bookkeeping, and the debt is paid in Chapter 2.6.

And you have four demonstrated failures of the force formulation, each one with a chapter attached. (a) Constraints: a page of algebra and an unwanted tension for the pendulum, answered by Chapter 1.2 §6 in three lines. (b) Coordinates: F=ma\vv F=m\vv aF=ma is not form invariant, and general relativity has no global Cartesian frame, answered by Chapter 1.2 §7 and spent in Chapter 3.2. (c) Fields: uncountably many degrees of freedom and no particles to sum forces over, answered by Chapter 5.2. (d) Quantum: there is no force operator, but there is a Hamiltonian, answered by Chapters 4.2 and 5.3.

Finally you have Fermat's template: one number per path, made stationary, yielding a local law at every point. It is coordinate-free, and it needs only a single scalar function, which are precisely the two things (b) and (c) lacked.

Where this gets spent. Chapter 1.2 generalises §5's template into the action principle and answers failures (a) and (b) at a stroke, giving constraints in three lines and form invariance under any change of coordinates at all. Chapter 1.3 Legendre-transforms that Lagrangian into a Hamiltonian and builds phase space on it. Chapter 1.4 acts on the same object with symmetries, and returns §2's energy and §3's momentum and angular momentum as theorems with named hypotheses, rather than as results read off the third law. Chapter 2.6 settles §3.3's crack by computing the momentum stored in the field between two moving charges and finding it is exactly what the particles lost. Chapter 3.2 spends failure (b) in earnest, building a physics with no global Cartesian frame anywhere in it. Chapter 5.2 spends failure (c), and Chapters 4.2 and 5.3 spend failure (d). From Chapter 1.2 to the end of this book, "solve this theory" will mean "write down its action and vary it".
